981.title: The resentment list
981.howItsDone: In Alcoholics Anonymous, members often write a resentment inventory with a sponsor's help, listing whom they resent, why, and what it affected, and then looking at their own part.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the drafts folder, a letter written whole and kept. Your line was said, not sent. Today, a different kind of writing: not one letter, but a list.

"He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me." That's not a police report. It's the third verse of the Dhammapada, the Buddhist collection of sayings, in Max Müller's translation. It sounds like something the mind says at night, on a loop, about a boss or a sibling or an ex: a list, recited from memory, item by item. The verse isn't asking anyone to pretend the list is false. It's pointing at what happens to the one who keeps reciting it. Today: the resentment list.
screen: `HE ABUSED ME, HE ROBBED ME.` → `A LIST, ON A LOOP.` → `WHAT HAPPENS TO THE ONE WHO RECITES IT.`

segments.voice: First, the verse finishes its sentence: "in those who harbour such thoughts hatred will never cease." The next verse repeats the same list and says that in those who do not harbor such thoughts, hatred will cease. The list is identical. What changes is harboring: keeping it docked, tied up and fed. Second, why paper helps. A list in your head never ends, because the mind keeps adding and repeating. A list on paper has edges. You can see there are five things, not five hundred, and that some are old and small. Alcoholics Anonymous makes a written practice of this. Its Big Book describes writing resentments down: who you resent, what happened, and what it touched in you. Then the uncomfortable part: an honest look at your own share, where there is one. Not to excuse anyone, but to see the whole picture. Third, a warning from the letter to the Hebrews: "lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and thereby many be defiled." A root works underground; you don't see it until it has spread. Writing the list digs it up into daylight, where it can be looked at instead of growing in the dark. Fourth, honesty. The list only works if it's true, petty ones included, the ones you'd be embarrassed to say aloud. Nobody grades it. The page can hold the same list the Dhammapada quotes, without the harboring.
screen: `HATRED WILL NEVER CEASE.` · `A LIST ON PAPER HAS EDGES.` · `A ROOT OF BITTERNESS.` · `WRITE THE PETTY ONES TOO.` · then, large: `ON PAPER.`

segments.voice: On a page, write three resentments, one per line: a name or a place, and in a few words what happened. Beside each, write what it touched, your pride, your money, your safety, your sense of being loved, and, if you're willing, whether any part of it was yours. Then look at the page for a few breaths, and notice that there are three lines, and that they stop.
Big Book. Alcoholics Anonymous's book, which describes writing resentments down honestly, so they can be seen instead of recited. Today's word.
Your line: on paper. A list with edges can be looked at instead of recited. See you tomorrow.

982.title: Forgiving parents
982.hook: forgiving parents, with honesty about what happened
982.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read the commandment to honor father and mother alongside the honest family stories of Genesis, and some teachers in both traditions distinguish honoring parents from approving everything they did.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Big Book's resentment list. Your line was on paper: a list with edges, looked at instead of recited. Today, the people none of us got to choose.

Genesis does not flatter its families. One verse sets up a household's trouble in a single sentence: "And Isaac loved Esau, because he did eat of his venison: but Rebekah loved Jacob." A father with a favorite. A mother with a different favorite. Two boys growing up under one roof. No gentle editing, no line about how they did their best. The text just says it. That honesty is a good place to start a hard subject. Today: forgiving parents.
screen: `GENESIS DOESN'T FLATTER.` → `A FATHER'S FAVORITE, A MOTHER'S FAVORITE.` → `THE TEXT JUST SAYS IT.`

segments.voice: First, honesty about what happened. Forgiving a parent doesn't begin with excuses. It begins the way Genesis does, by naming it. The story that follows, of tricks, a stolen blessing and a brother who has to flee, shows what the favoritism cost. Second, the pattern travels. Years later Jacob has sons of his own, and Genesis says: "Now Israel loved Joseph more than all his children, because he was the son of his old age: and he made him a coat of many colours." Israel is Jacob's other name. The favored son becomes the father who plays favorites. The coat is the same wound, handed down in brighter cloth. Third, today's line. They were young too. A parent who hurts a child was once a child in someone else's house, learning love the way it was shown there. Jacob learned favoritism as the favorite. Seeing that doesn't make the hurt smaller. It makes the person who caused it more human, a link in a chain rather than a monster at the top of one. Fourth, honoring is not approving. The commandment says "Honour thy father and thy mother." Some Jewish and Christian teachers point out that it asks for honor, not agreement, and not pretending. And nothing here asks anyone to forgive abuse on a timetable, or to go back somewhere unsafe. Where real harm happened, forgiveness, if it comes, can come slowly and from a distance. Today is for something smaller.
screen: `ISAAC LOVED ESAU, REBEKAH LOVED JACOB.` · `THE FAVORITE BECOMES THE FATHER.` · `A LINK IN A CHAIN.` · `HONOR IS NOT APPROVAL.` · then, large: `THEY WERE YOUNG TOO.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one parent, or whoever raised you; if that relationship holds deep harm, choose someone else, or simply rest in the breath, which is a full practice too. Otherwise, name one small thing of theirs that still stings, a phrase, a missed game, a habit, then picture them young, before you, being taught by their own parents. Hold both at once: this happened, and they were young too.
Forgiving parents. Naming honestly what happened, and seeing the person who did it as someone who was once a child too. Today's word.
Your line: they were young too. Naming it and seeing them whole can both be true. Until tomorrow.

983.title: The dead
983.hook: you can forgive someone who has died
983.howItsDone: The Talmud describes going to the grave of someone you wronged and saying aloud, before others, that you wronged them; some people visit graves to speak to those they've lost, sometimes to settle what was left unsaid.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forgiving parents. Your line was they were young too: a link in a chain, not a monster at the top. Today, the people who can no longer hear an apology, or offer one.

A phone still holds a voicemail from someone who has died. It's two years old, about nothing, a question about dinner. And underneath it sits an argument that was never settled, because there was supposed to be time. Now there isn't. The person who could apologize is gone, and so is the person who could hear one. It's easy to assume the door has closed. Some very old texts say otherwise. Today: the dead.
screen: `A VOICEMAIL ABOUT NOTHING.` → `AN ARGUMENT NEVER SETTLED.` → `IS THE DOOR CLOSED?`

segments.voice: First, a king who gets the news. In the second book of Samuel, King David's son Absalom has turned against him, raised an army and driven his father out of Jerusalem. In the battle that follows, Absalom is killed. David doesn't celebrate a victory. He goes up to a room over the gate and weeps: "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee." A son who tried to take his father's throne, and the father's cry is his name, over and over. Whatever lay between them, David's love goes on speaking to his son after he is gone. Second, the other direction. The Talmud records a teaching for someone who wronged a person who has since died. They can't go and appease the person anymore, so they bring others to the grave and say there, aloud, that they wronged this person. The words are still worth saying, in a place, with witnesses. Third, forgiving the dead. If an apology can be offered to the dead, forgiveness can be too. The other person doesn't need to take part. Forgiveness, as this whole block has been saying, happens in the one who forgives, and saying it aloud gives it a time and a place. Fourth, what it doesn't require: pretending they were someone else. Absalom still rebelled. Forgiving the dead is releasing what you're still holding, not rewriting who they were.
screen: `O MY SON ABSALOM.` · `WORDS SPOKEN AT THE GRAVE.` · `THEY DON'T NEED TO TAKE PART.` · `RELEASE, NOT REWRITE.` · then, large: `IT STILL COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has died, with whom something was left unsettled; if that's too heavy today, choose something small, or simply sit with their memory. If you can, say quietly what you forgive them for, one sentence is enough, or move your lips without sound if you're not alone. Then sit with whatever comes, and if you pray, you can name them in your prayer.
The dead. Forgiveness, or an apology, offered to someone who has died, spoken in a time and place, even though they can't answer. Today's word.
Your line: it still counts. They can't answer, and the words still matter. Day nine hundred eighty-three, done.

984.title: Angry with God
984.hook: Job and the psalmists were allowed to be angry with God (Psalm 22:1)
984.howItsDone: Jews and Christians pray the psalms of lament, including Psalm 22, and some teachers in both traditions point to Job and the lament psalms as a model for bringing anger and complaint honestly to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dead, and words still worth saying at a grave. Your line was it still counts. Today, the hardest place some people's anger goes: upward.

"My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Those are the first words of Psalm 22. Not a hymn of thanks, not a calm reflection: a cry, aimed straight at God, asking why. And it sits inside the Bible's own prayer book, kept and prayed. It wasn't filed away as an embarrassing moment or softened into something more polite. It was left exactly as raw as it is, for anyone who would ever need those words. Today: angry with God.
screen: `WHY HAST THOU FORSAKEN ME?` → `A CRY, NOT A HYMN.` → `KEPT IN THE PRAYER BOOK.`

segments.voice: First, the psalm keeps going: "why art thou so far from helping me, and from the words of my roaring?" Roaring, not whispering. The psalm does move later toward trust and praise, but it doesn't skip the roar to get there. And in Matthew and Mark, Jesus cries its opening line from the cross. Second, Job. He loses his children, his wealth, his health, and his friends arrive with explanations. Job refuses them: "I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul." Chapter after chapter, he demands that God answer him. Third, the surprise. When God finally speaks, out of the whirlwind, Job is pressed hard with questions. But as the book closes, God's anger turns on the friends who defended God so neatly: "ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath." Readers differ about what that means. One reading: honest anger, brought to God, counts as a kind of faithfulness, and pretending does not. Fourth, the prophet Habakkuk opens his book the same way: "O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!" Again, it's kept, as scripture. Some people who pray hear these texts as a permission. For people who don't, there's still something here: anger at loss and unfairness is allowed to be said out loud, rather than buried.
screen: `THE WORDS OF MY ROARING.` · `I WILL NOT REFRAIN MY MOUTH.` · `JOB SPOKE RIGHTLY.` · `HOW LONG SHALL I CRY?` · then, large: `HONEST IS ALLOWED.`

segments.voice: Find one honest complaint, something that seems unfair or a loss that never made sense, and don't tidy it. If God is part of your life, say it to God plainly, the way the psalm does: why? If not, say it to life, or the night sky, or just the room, once, then stay in the quiet that follows; nothing has to answer.
Habakkuk. One of the prophets whose honest complaint, carried straight to God, scripture keeps rather than softens. Today's word.
Your line: honest is allowed. The psalm, Job and Habakkuk all kept the true version. That's day nine hundred eighty-four.

985.title: Forgiving institutions
985.hook: forgiving a church, a company, a country is different from forgiving a person
985.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Daniel 9 as a model of confessing wrongs on behalf of a whole people, and some communities and institutions today issue collective apologies for past harms while victims decide for themselves whether and how to forgive.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Habakkuk, and the honest complaints scripture keeps. Your line was honest is allowed. Today, anger aimed at something with no single face.

A hospital billing office. A school that looked away. A congregation that closed ranks. A company that laid off a whole floor by email. A government office that lost the file, again. When the hurt comes from one of these, who exactly is there to forgive? The receptionist didn't write the policy. The pastor who's there now wasn't there then. The building can't apologize. Today: forgiving institutions.
screen: `NO SINGLE FACE.` → `WHO WROTE THE POLICY?` → `THE BUILDING CAN'T APOLOGIZE.`

segments.voice: First, a prayer in the plural. In the book of Daniel, Daniel prays for his whole people: "We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled." We, not I. He names the kings, the princes and the fathers who came before him, and still says we. In Daniel's prayer, wrong can belong to a group, not just to one person. Second, the trouble. When a person hurts you, you can forgive that person. When an institution hurts you, the hurt is spread across a policy, a culture, many hands and a lot of silence. Forgiving it can feel like trying to hug fog. Third, a way through. Henry David Thoreau, in his essay on civil disobedience, observes that it's said a corporation has no conscience, but a corporation of conscientious people has one. Institutions are made of people. Some find it possible to release bitterness toward the individuals inside, who may be doing their best, while still naming what the institution as a whole did. Fourth, forgiveness isn't dropping the matter. You can let go of the poison you carry about a church, a company or a country, and still write the letter, file the complaint, vote, or speak up so it doesn't happen to the next person. In Daniel, the confession and the plea for things to be put right come in the same breath. In this way of seeing it, the letting go is for the one who was hurt, and the accountability is for whoever comes next.
screen: `WE HAVE SINNED.` · `LIKE TRYING TO HUG FOG.` · `A CORPORATION WITH A CONSCIENCE.` · `RELEASE IT, STILL SPEAK UP.` · then, large: `BIGGER THAN ONE.`

segments.voice: Name silently one institution that has hurt you, a school, a workplace, a religious community, an agency, and notice where the anger sits in your body. Picture one ordinary person inside it who had nothing to do with what happened to you, and see if you can let just them off the hook. Then, separately, name one thing you'd still want the institution to own or change; both can stay true.
Forgiving institutions. Releasing bitterness toward a group with no single face, while still asking it to own what it did. Today's word.
Your line: bigger than one. Kindness for the person in front of you, the complaint for the place it belongs. See you tomorrow.

deciding no one is to blame because many people were involved
forgiving the whole group because one person there apologized

986.title: Boundaries after
986.hook: forgiveness and safety can go together
986.howItsDone: Some counselors, pastors and rabbis teach that forgiveness does not require trusting someone again right away, and point to Joseph's testing of his brothers in Genesis 42–45 as a story of forgiveness that waited to see change.

segments.voice: Yesterday, forgiving institutions. Your line was bigger than one: release the bitterness, keep asking for change. Today, the question after forgiving anyone: then what?

A woman forgives her brother for borrowing money and never paying it back. She means it; the bitterness is gone. A month later he calls, warm and friendly, and asks to borrow again. Here's the question that can trip people up: if she's really forgiven him, doesn't she have to say yes? Doesn't saying no mean she's still holding it against him? Genesis has a story about a man who tested the lock before he opened the door to his brothers. Today: boundaries after.
screen: `THE BITTERNESS IS GONE.` → `HE ASKS AGAIN.` → `DOES FORGIVING MEAN YES?`

segments.voice: First, Joseph. His brothers sold him into slavery. Years later he's governor in Egypt, and in a famine the same brothers arrive to buy grain. They don't recognize him. He recognizes them, and he doesn't rush to embrace them. He tests them. He keeps one brother as a hostage, then frames the youngest, Benjamin, and watches what the others will do. Will they abandon this brother the way they abandoned him? Second, the answer. Judah, the brother who once suggested selling Joseph, offers to stay as a slave in Benjamin's place. Only then does Joseph break down: "I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt." He weeps and kisses his brothers, after he has watched what they do. One way to read the testing: he waited to see whether they had changed before he let them close. Third, the wisdom books are practical about safety. Proverbs says: "Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go: Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul." That isn't hatred. It's caution. Some people aren't safe to walk beside, and the texts don't ask anyone to pretend otherwise. Fourth, how the two fit. Forgiveness lives inside you: you let go of the debt, the bitterness, the replay. A boundary lives in what you do: what you lend, where you go, when you answer the phone. The sister can forgive her brother completely and still say: I'm not lending money again. That's not a grudge. It's a door with a lock.
screen: `JOSEPH TESTS HIS BROTHERS.` · `WHOM YE SOLD INTO EGYPT.` · `WITH A FURIOUS MAN THOU SHALT NOT GO.` · `INSIDE, AND IN WHAT YOU DO.` · then, large: `FORGIVE AND STAY SAFE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you've forgiven, or are trying to, where something still needs protecting: your time, your money, your peace, your body. Name the boundary in one plain sentence, like I leave when the shouting starts, or I don't answer after ten at night, and say it silently, without anger. Notice that you can wish them well and still keep it, and if you pray, pray for them and for your own safety in the same breath.
Boundaries after. Letting go of the bitterness inside, while still protecting what needs protecting in what you do. Today's word.
Your line: forgive and stay safe. Letting go and locking the door can both be kind. Day nine hundred eighty-six, done.

987.title: Forgiving strangers
987.hook: the driver who cut in, the rude clerk
987.howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Proverbs and Ecclesiastes among the Bible's wisdom books; Proverbs 19:11, on passing over an offense, is sometimes quoted when people talk about letting small slights go.

segments.voice: Yesterday, boundaries after. Your line was forgive and stay safe. This week held lists, parents, the dead, God and whole institutions. Today, the smallest hurts of all, from people you'll never see again.

The light turns green, and a gray hatchback slides into the lane with no signal, close enough to touch. A horn goes off. Later, at the pharmacy counter, the clerk sighs, doesn't look up, and pushes the bag across without a word. Neither knows your name. Neither will think of you again. And yet these two can follow someone around for a whole afternoon, retold at dinner, replayed in the shower. Today belongs to the small hurts, the strangers. Two short sayings from the Bible's wisdom books have a plan for them.
screen: `NO SIGNAL. NO LOOK.` → `TWO STRANGERS, ONE AFTERNOON.` → `TWO OLD SAYINGS.`

segments.voice: First, a proverb. Proverbs nineteen says, in the King James words: "The discretion of a man deferreth his anger; and it is his glory to pass over a transgression." Deferreth: puts off, slows down. The anger isn't banned. It's made to wait, long enough for good sense to catch up. Second, the verb: pass over. Not punish, not report, not retell at dinner. The picture is walking past something on the road, the way the gray hatchback is already three blocks away. And the proverb doesn't call this weakness. It calls it glory. Third, a mirror, from Ecclesiastes. It advises against straining to hear every word said about you, or you may hear your own servant cursing you, and it gives the reason: "For oftentimes also thine own heart knoweth that thou thyself likewise hast cursed others." The clerk is having a day. So have you, and on some of those days someone else was the stranger on the receiving end. Fourth, passing over isn't pretending. Cutting someone off is still dangerous. Rudeness is still rude. It just means not carrying a stranger home. They were a stranger at breakfast; they don't need to become a roommate in your head by dinner.
screen: `ANGER, MADE TO WAIT.` · `PASS OVER IT.` · `YOU'VE HAD DAYS TOO.` · `DON'T CARRY THEM HOME.` · then, large: `THEY'RE HAVING A DAY.`

segments.voice: Bring back one stranger from the last few days, a driver, a caller, someone in a line, and see the moment clearly, just once. Then let the picture widen: they woke up somewhere this morning, with a kitchen, a phone full of messages, a problem you know nothing about. You don't have to like what they did; just let them be a whole person with a whole day. On an out-breath, let them go back to that day without you, and if you pray, you can include them in your prayer.
Forgiving strangers. Letting go quickly of small hurts from people you'll never meet again, without pretending they were fine. Today's word.
Your line: they're having a day. So have you, sometimes. That's day nine hundred eighty-seven.

original.note: Hebrew, Proverbs 19:11: to pass over, to go by or across.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgiving strangers means being a pushover.
what it means: letting the anger wait, remembering your own bad days, and not carrying the stranger home.
what a scholar hears: Proverbs 19:11 uses avor, an everyday Hebrew verb for passing by or crossing over, so the offense is pictured as something you walk past.
